examples.question_text: A fair coin is tossed three times. Write the complementary event to ‘at least one head’.
examples.solution_text:
The complement of ‘at least one’ is ‘none’.
The complementary event is ‘no heads’, so all three tosses show tails.

examples.question_text: Four batteries are tested. The probability that none is flat is $\frac{7}{12}$. Find the probability that at least one battery is flat.
examples.solution_text:
The complement of ‘at least one flat battery’ is ‘no flat batteries’.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one flat})&=1-P(\text{none flat})\\&=1-\frac{7}{12}\\&=\frac{5}{12}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A student enters two races. Her probabilities of winning are $0.7$ and $0.5$, independently. Find the probability that she wins at least one race, as a decimal.
A fair six-sided die is rolled three times. Find the probability of rolling at least one $5$, as a fraction in simplest form.
examples.solution_text:
The complement is ‘no rolls show $5$’. Each roll has probability $\frac{5}{6}$ of not showing $5$. The rolls are independent.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{no fives})&=\frac{5}{6}\times\frac{5}{6}\times\frac{5}{6}\\&=\frac{125}{216}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one five})&=1-\frac{125}{216}\\&=\frac{91}{216}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A bag contains $4$ red and $6$ blue counters. Two counters are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability of drawing at least one red counter.
examples.solution_text:
The complement is ‘both counters are blue’. After a blue counter is drawn, $5$ blue counters remain among $9$ counters.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{both blue})&=\frac{6}{10}\times\frac{5}{9}\\&=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one red})&=1-\frac{1}{3}\\&=\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A bag contains $5$ red and $7$ blue marbles. Three marbles are selected at random without replacement. Find the probability that at least one is red.
examples.solution_text:
The complement is ‘all three marbles are blue’. Along this path, the blue count and total each decrease by one after every draw.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{all blue})&=\frac{7}{12}\times\frac{6}{11}\times\frac{5}{10}\\&=\frac{7}{44}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one red})&=1-\frac{7}{44}\\&=\frac{37}{44}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Three light globes work independently. Their probabilities of working are $0.9$, $0.8$ and $0.95$. Find the probability that at least one globe does not work.
examples.solution_text:
The complement of ‘at least one does not work’ is ‘all three work’.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{all work})&=0.9\times0.8\times0.95\\&=0.684\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one does not work})&=1-P(\text{all work})\\&=1-0.684\\&=0.316\end{aligned}$
